confidence_note: Book text not available. The economics (acquisition cost, base profit, cost savings, referrals, price premium, pay for new customers) come from a reader summary and publisher copy; the exact percentages disagree between sources, so they are hedged. The old text's 'five times more expensive' ratio, 'several new customers per loyal one' and year-by-year spending pattern are not attributable and were dropped. The retention-profit estimate is flagged as contested by a 1992 Carrol and Reichheld paper noted on Wikipedia.
facts: Senior managers are often pulled into sales proposals for new accounts, which inflates acquisition cost, and most help desk calls come from new customers (reader summary).

A loyal customer adds base profit, cost savings, referrals and a price premium; once these are counted, acquisition cost can turn negative. In mature companies 20% to 30% of acquisition spending is often wasteful.
Prospects who arrive by referral close at significantly higher rates than walk-in customers.

Many companies pay salespeople for winning new customers rather than keeping existing ones; salespeople who do not expect to stay have little reason to pursue repeat business; the sales channel should attract the right customers, not just many. A typical company loses 10% to 30% of its customers a year.

The jacket claims a small gain in retention can double profits; a reader summary puts it as a 5% rise in retention raising an average customer's value by 25% to 100%; an earlier Reichheld and Sasser (1990) calculation gives 25% to 85%.
Caveat: Carrol and Reichheld (1992) disputed some of these retention-to-profit calculations as resting on faulty cross-sectional analysis (Wikipedia, Loyalty business model).
scene_details: a senior manager writing a sales proposal for a new account
help desk calls from new customers
a bonus for new accounts only
tension: A company pays for the arrival of customers while most of the profit comes from the ones who stay.
opening_idea: Open on the pay structure: the person who wins a customer is paid, the person who keeps one often is not.

lessons.idea: What you pay or praise decides what people chase; reward keeping as well as winning.
lessons.anchor: Salespeople paid for new customers, not retention.
lessons.example: A cafe bonus for loyalty-card sign-ups while nobody is thanked for remembering a regular.

reflect_final: In your work or friendships, where do you put effort into winning someone new while the person who stayed gets taken for granted?

use_cases.situation: The sales bonus plan is being set.
use_cases.move: Point out that you pay for new accounts and ask what it would take to also reward renewals and referrals.

use_cases.situation: You are about to spend the week chasing new clients.
use_cases.move: Remember that most help desk calls come from new customers and first reach out to a regular you haven't talked to in a while.

use_cases.situation: A colleague closed a new account while a longtime client's renewal slips.
use_cases.move: Celebrate the win, then propose a date to talk with the client who has been there longest.

pocket_idea: Winning a customer is the expensive part; keeping one is where the profit builds. Reward both.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: In many companies the person who wins a customer gets the bonus and the one who keeps them gets nothing, which Reichheld argues is backwards.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Reichheld looks at what a customer costs and brings: new customers are expensive to win, loyal ones add base profit, savings, referrals and a price premium; yet many firms pay salespeople only for new accounts.
